nickname: California to fed enviro regulators: Explain yourself
proper_title: California Air Resources Board v. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: In September of 2018, the California Air Resources Board filed Freedom of Information Act requests with two federal agencies asking for the technical analyses they used to justify a reversal of Obama-era emission and fuel economy standards. The California’s Attorney General is now suing the agencies—the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration—on behalf of the Board. In the suit, the state argues that the agencies violated the Freedom of Information Act by failing to adequately respond to the requests, withholding information based on “inadequate justification” or no justification at all.

proper_title: State of California v. Donald Trump
case_summary: In one of his first acts as president, Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring that the costs associated with any new federal regulation "be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least two prior regulations." Three states sued, led by California. They argued that the order was an overreach of executive authority, since regulations are based on laws passed by Congress and that it violates various federal laws that govern how regulations are written and enforced. In April 2020, a panel of appeals court judges dismissed the case, ruling that because it wasn't clear that the executive order actually led to a change in federal policy, the states didn't have the right bring the case in the first place.

proper_title: State of California v. Alex Azar
case_summary: In February of 2019, the Trump administration introduced a new set of restrictions on the federal Title X Family Planning program that would block funding to any organization that offers abortions or refers patients to abortion providers. The State of California sued, arguing that the new rule violates various federal laws, including the Affordable Care Act, as well as the constitutional rights of pregnant women to equal protection under the law. Both a district and appellate court sided with the Trump administration. A coalition of 21 other states filed a separate lawsuit.

proper_title: State of Washington v. Trump
case_summary: After hitting a judicial wall the first two times, the Trump administration made a third attempt at a travel ban—it permanently blocks immigration from citizens of eight countries. California joins five other states in once again taking the policy to court.

proper_title: People of the State of California v. United States of America
case_summary: In a solo lawsuit, California claimed that in waiving certain environmental laws in order to speed up construction of the much-promised international barrier on the Mexico border, the federal government violated state and federal environmental law, as well as the state’s “economic interests, procedural rights, and sovereignty.” A district judge disagreed, as did a panel of appeals court judges.

proper_title: State of New York vs. U.S. Department of Energy
case_summary: California joined New York in suing the Department of Energy for a new rule allowing the agency to offer interim waivers for energy efficiency tests. The coalition of states argue that the new rule exceeds the DOE’s authority.

proper_title: State of New York vs. U.S. Department of Interior and the Fish and Wildlife and Service
case_summary: California, New York and other states are challenging the Trump administration’s final rule that limits the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. The final rule says migratory birds are not protected from incidental harm by oil companies, developers and other human activities. The states argue that rule is in conflict with the language and purpose of the act.

nickname: Calculating costs and benefits of Clean Air Act regulations
proper_title: State of New York vs. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: California and other states are suing the Trump administration over how the Environmental Protection Agency calculates the costs and benefits of Clean Air Act regulations. The final rule will require the EPA to produce a more detailed cost-benefit analysis, weighing the cost to an industry against the societal and environmental impacts, before creating new regulations.

nickname: Greenhouse gas emissions from stationary sources
proper_title: State of California vs. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: Leading a coalition of 27 states and municipalities, California is suing the Trump administration for its final rule that replaces a new threshold for determining if an industry is a significant source of greenhouse gases. The rule says if the industry emits less than 3% of total U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, it cannot be regulated under section 111 of the Clean Air Act. California argues that the EPA didn’t follow administrative procedures when it created this rule.

proper_title: State of New York vs. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: California and 15 other attorney generals are suing the Trump administration for not strengthening air quality standards for ozone, a key ingredient of smog. The lawsuit argues the Environmental Protection Agency ignored new evidence that confirms how detrimental ozone exposure can be to people’s health. California has the worst ozone pollution in the nation.

proper_title: State of New York vs. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: The Trump administration posted a final rule directing the Environmental Protection Agency to give less weight to scientific studies when the underlying data are not publicly available for independent review. EPA regularly uses epidemiological studies that rely on health data that is confidential and not publically available for review. California and several other states argue that the rule undermines future EPA rules related to public health and the environment.

nickname: Energy efficiency standards for washers and dryers
proper_title: State of California vs. U.S. Department of Energy
case_summary: California and 14 other states are suing the Trump administration for creating a class of washers and dryers based on cycle time, which exempts them from existing energy efficiency standards. The states argue that by carving out a time-based class for washers and dryers, the administration violates the Energy Policy Conservation Act’s provision that prohibits the Energy Department from “prescrib[ing] any amended standard which increases the maximum allowable energy use . . . of a covered product.”

nickname: Limiting habitat protection under the Endangered Species Act
proper_title: State of California vs. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
case_summary: The Trump administration recently approved two final rules making it more difficult to protect critical habitat for endangered animals and plants. Under the changes, federal officials have a narrower definition of habitat and exclude some areas from protection. In the lawsuit, California and 17 other states argue that the new rules violate federal laws. California has more than 300 species protected by the Endangered Species Act.

proper_title: State of California vs. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: California and 12 other states are suing the EPA for changing a federal rule that required large air polluters such as oil refineries and chemical plants to permanently take actions to reduce their emissions. Under the new rule, they would escape some federal air pollution regulations when they keep their total emissions under 10 tons a year.

proper_title: State of California vs. U.S. Department of Education
case_summary: Under a new federal rule, schools can automatically receive federal dollars if the Education Department doesn’t take action on a school’s certification within 12 months, and there’s no longer a cap on how much instruction can be outsourced to a school with a common owner. California argues that the new rules run afoul of federal requirements to participate in federal student-aid programs.

proper_title: State of California vs. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: California and several other states are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s final rule on greenhouse gas regulations for airplanes. The states say the regulations would not reduce emissions and would just amount to business-as-usual. They also argue that they lock in meaningless standards for years, given how long it will take for manufacturers to design compliant aircrafts.

proper_title: State of California vs. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: California, 16 other states and the City of New York are challenging the Trump administration's decision not to strengthen health standards for fine particles of soot. California’s air has the nation’s worst levels of particulates, which have been linked to heart attacks and lung disease. The states argue that the EPA conducted a flawed review and that the available science shows that the standards should be strengthened to protect public health.

proper_title: State of New York vs. the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
case_summary:
As more states are capping interest rates on loans from non-bank lenders like payday loans and title loan companies, lenders have found a way around state laws by partnering with national banks. National banks are only bound by laws regulating interest rates in the state where they’re located, so some lenders are partnering with them to avoid the regulations.
California, six other states and the District of Columbia are challenging the federal rule.

nickname: Exempting some dishwashers from energy efficiency standards
proper_title: State of California vs. United States Department of Energy
case_summary: The Trump administration issued a final rule that exempts certain residential dishwashers from energy efficiency standards. California Attorney General Xavier Becerra, 15 attorneys general and the city of New York are challenging the rule.

proper_title: State of New York vs. United States Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: Under President Barack Obama, the Environmental Protection Agency established a 100-foot zone that must be clear of people, regardless of property boundaries, whenever pesticides are applied. In October, the Trump administration limited this zone, allowing pesticides to be applied as long as no one is within the farm’s boundaries. Five states have joined California in the lawsuit.

proper_title: State of New York vs. United States Department of Energy
case_summary: Federal law requires that the Department of Energy periodically review its energy efficiency standards, which cover more than 60 categories of home appliances and other products. New York, California, 12 other states, the District of Columbia and New York City, claim that the energy department is violating the law by not conducting a timely review and updating standards in 25 categories.

proper_title: State of California v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security
case_summary: After the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Trump administration could not revoke protections for so-called “dreamers” under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), acting Department of Homeland Security secretary Chad Wolf issued a memo restricting the program. DACA offers people who were illegally brought to the U.S. as children a pathway to stay in the country. But the memo limited the time recipients could apply for deferred action and work authorizations, and placed restrictions on those who travel abroad. California, Maine, Maryland and Minnesota are challenging the memo in court, arguing that the administration did not consider how the restrictions would affect DACA recipients, as required by law. They also claim that that Wolf used flawed logic to justify the change and that the memo is invalid because he has not been confirmed by the Senate.

proper_title: State of California v. Janet Dhillon
case_summary: Under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is required to provide employment data to state and local agencies that protect people from work and housing discrimination. The data is required to be openly available upon request and without cost. Anti-disrimination agencies, including the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing, rely on the data to identify civil rights violations and prioritize investigations. Under the Trump administration, the federal commission has limited access to that data and won’t provide it until a specific employer is already under investigation. California and its Department of Fair Employment and Housing are suing. They argue that the federal agency’s actions are part of a broader effort to limit access to important employment data, and that they violate the Civil Rights Act. Maryland, Minnesota and its Department of Human Rights have also joined the lawsuit.

proper_title: State of California v. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives
case_summary: Unfinished pistol frames and rifle receivers are used to make “ghost guns.” Because the frames are incomplete and require assembly, they don’t fall under firearm rules regulated by the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. In California, “ghost guns” have been used in several high-profile shootings including one in Santa Clarita last year. A 16-year-old student shot five other classmates, ultimately killing two students and himself. California, along with the Giffords Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence, are suing the federal ATF because it doesn’t regulate the unfinished frames and receivers as firearms. Parents of the two students killed in the 2019 school shooting have also joined the lawsuit. They argue that the federal agency’s position on “ghost guns” disregards the Gun Control Act.

nickname: Rolling back rules on methane emissions
proper_title: State of California v. Andrew R. Wheeler
case_summary: In August, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency rolled back Obama-era emission standards that limited methane emissions caused by oil and natural gas production. The rollbacks will likely lead to increased methane emissions — about 850,000 tons more between 2021 and 2030, the federal agency estimates. California is suing, along with the California Air Resources Board, 19 other states and the District of Columbia. They argue that the latest rules violate the Clean Air Act and abandon methane regulations without any justification.

proper_title: State of California v. Council on Environmental Quality
case_summary: Under the National Environmental Policy Act, federal agencies must consider the environmental impacts of their actions, which include approving energy projects and deciding the management of federal public lands. In California, state agencies have used the policy to provide input on the Trump administration’s proposal to raise the height of the Shasta Dam, which could impact nearby wildlife and the McCloud River. In July, the federal Council on Environmental Quality announced a rule that reduces required scrutiny. This allows the federal government more freedom to make environmental decisions, while taking less time to consider the impact. California, Washington, 19 other states, Washington D.C. and Guam are suing. Jurisdictions in New York, Connecticut and Texas have joined the lawsuit too. They argue that the rule is arbitrary and undermines the intent of the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act, and that the Council on Environmental Quality overstepped its authority.

proper_title: Commonwealth of Pennsylvania v. Louis DeJoy
case_summary: Soon after President Trump appointed him to head the U.S. Postal Service in May 2020, Louis DeJoy began making changes at the nation’s mail delivery system. That included limiting overtime for mail carriers and restricting the number of trips a carrier can make each day. DeJoy has said that these changes are meant to cut costs at the cash-strapped service. But given the upcoming presidential election, Trump’s clear hostility toward wide-scale voting-by-mail and reports of delayed deliveries, Democrats accuse DeJoy of undermining the 2020 election. Pennsylvania, California, four other states and Washington DC sued. They argue that the changes violate federal postal laws requiring the efficient and reliable delivery of mail, and provisions of the U.S. Constitution that give states the right to regulate their own elections and protects the voting rights of older Americans, who disproportionately vote by mail.

proper_title: People of the State of California v. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
case_summary: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation is the national agency tasked with keeping savings and checking accounts safe. If a federally regulated bank goes out of business, the FDIC insure those accounts are secure up to a certain amount. In exchange for that protection, the agency restricts the types of risks that deposit-accepting banks can take. Those regulations typically take precedence over state regulations, like caps on the interest that banks can charge borrowers. But in June 2020, the FDIC added a tweak to that rule: not only would its regulations supersede interest caps for banks, but any financial institution that buys loans from those banks. California law caps the interest rate non-bank lenders can charge at 450% for small payday loans and a little over 30% for loans between $255 and $10,000. In a lawsuit, filed along with prosecutors from six states and the District of Columbia, the California Department of Justice argued that the new rule will “facilitate predatory lending through sham ‘rent-a-bank’ partnerships,” in which high-cost lenders get around state law by buying loans from FDIC-regulated banks. The new rule, the suit argues, violates federal banking law and exceeds the FDIC’s authority.

proper_title: State of Maryland v United States Department of Transportation
case_summary: In late August 2020, the Trump administration gave the green light for freight companies to begin transporting liquefied natural gas in bulk along the nation’s rail network. The new rule is meant to make it easier for U.S. energy companies to export natural gas. But the prospect of hundreds of thousands of gallons of explosive material regularly barrelling along the country’s freight corridors has given some state attorneys general pause. One of those is California’s Xavier Becerra, who sued the U.S. Department of Transportation with 13 other states and Washington D.C. The litigants argue that the administration introduced the new rule without conducting a proper environmental and safety analysis.

proper_title: State of California v. Donald Trump
case_summary: Every 10 years, the U.S. Constitution requires the federal government to conduct a census. One of the goals in tallying up the “whole number of persons in each State”  is to decide how to divvy up Congressional representation and federal funding. On July 21, 2020, President Trump issued a memorandum directing federal people-counters to exclude undocumented immigrants. The state of California; the cities of Los Angeles, Long Beach and Oakland; and the Los Angeles Unified School District, sued. They argue that the term “whole number of persons” makes no mention of immigration status and that the president overstepped his authority in reinterpreting the provision. They also argue that the change in policy could cost California, with its large population of immigrants, “at least one seat in the U.S. House of Representatives” and significant federal funding.

proper_title: State of California v. Andrew Wheeler
case_summary: For decades states have used a particular provision of the Clean Water Act to delay, impose conditions on and deny major infrastructure projects, like oil and gas pipelines, that might threaten local water quality. But the federal Environmental Protection Agency — following an April 2019 executive order from President Donald Trump — is trying to blunt that tool. In July 2020, the agency issued a new interpretation of the regulation, putting a cap on how long projects may be delayed and limiting the scope of the objections that states can raise. In announcing the revision, EPA Administrator Andrew Wheeler said the goal was “to curb abuses of the Clean Water Act that have held our nation’s energy infrastructure projects hostage.” California, 19 other states and the District of Columbia sued. They argue that the rule violates the text and intent of the Clean Water Act,that the EPA failed to offer a compelling rationale for the change and that the agency overstepped its authority.

proper_title: Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. United States Department of Environmental Protection
case_summary: In May 2020, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency decided that regulating mercury and other toxic air pollutants that are emitted by coal- and oil-fired power plants is not "appropriate and necessary." The Trump administration’s new policy takes its cue from a 2015 Supreme Court ruling that scolded the nation’s top environmental regulators for failing to consider the costs of enforcing regulations that limit emissions of mercury, arsenic and other toxic pollutants. Though the Obama administration’s EPA performed a new analysis in 2016 and found that, those costs withstanding, the benefits of regulating these emissions outweigh the costs, the Trump administration has come to a different conclusion. Confusingly enough, this does not put an end to the regulation of these pollutants outright. But critics of the move say it puts the regulation of these emissions on a much weaker legal footing. Massachusetts, California, 18 states, the District of Columbia, Baltimore, Chicago, New York City and Erie County in upstate New York sued the EPA. They argue that the federal Clean Air Act requires federal regulators to keep such emissions in check and that the EPA’s new cost-benefit analysis that led to its new conclusion was sloppy and politically motivated.

proper_title: State of New York v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
case_summary: The Affordable Care Act included a nondiscrimination provision that barred hospitals, insurance companies and other health care systems that get federal funding from discriminating against their patients and clients based on race, color, national origin, sex, disability or age. The Obama administration’s Department of Health and Human Services interpreted that clause to include discrimination against transgender and gender non-conforming individuals and against patients who have had abortions or are seeking reproductive health care. The Trump administration has taken a different view, arguing that that is an overly broad interpretation of the Obamacare provision that could infringe on religious liberties. In June 2020, the Trump Health and Human Services Department issued a new rule, stripping out any reference to gender identity or abortion. New York, California, twenty other states and the District of Columbia sued. They argue that the new, narrower interpretation violates both the Affordable Care Act and the 1964 Civil Rights Act, that the Department overstepped its authority by creating new religious exemptions to the health care law and that it “runs counter to the evidence before the agency, disregards material facts and evidence, and fails to consider important aspects of the problem, including patient harms.”

nickname: Borrower Defense Rule, Round 2: An "insurmountable burden"
proper_title: Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Education
case_summary: Remember back in July 2017 when Massachusetts, California, and attorneys general sued the Trump administration’s Department of Education for its decision to delay the enactment of the “borrower defense rule”? That was the Obama-era regulation that made it easier for former students of fraudulent universities and colleges to have their loans forgiven. Since then, Secretary of Education Betsy Devos has introduced her own rule. The Devos regulation made it harder for former students to get debt relief, requiring them, for example, to prove that their former college knowingly misled them. The rule was panned not only by education advocates, veterans groups and Democrats, but some Republican as well. Both the House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate passed a resolution to reverse the rule, but it was vetoed by President Trump. So Massachusetts, California and 20 other states and jurisdictions sued again. In their lawsuit the attorneys general argue that the new rule creates an “insurmountable burden” for scammed students, that the Department of Education failed to provide a legal or rational justification for the new rule and that it violates federal education law.

nickname: International students: Go to class or go home
proper_title: State of California v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security
case_summary: Roughly 400,000 students from around the world attend universities, colleges and vocational schools in the United States, about 32,000 in California. The visas of those students are managed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement within the Department of Homeland Security. On July 6, ICE announced that it would no longer permit students who are attending schools that operate entirely online to stay in the country. Following a separate lawsuit brought by universities on the east coast, California filed its own. The state argues that the new regulation, introduced in the middle of a pandemic, is not only “cruel” but lacks a compelling logical or legal rationale. The state also argues that the U.S. immigration authorities introduced the rule without allowing for public comment, another violation of federal law. On July 14, 2020, the Trump administration rescinded the order.

proper_title: State of Michigan v Elisabeth D. Devos
case_summary: In late March, Congress passed the CARES Act, a $2 trillion aid package to help the country weather the coronavirus pandemic. Roughly $13.2 billion was set aside to help elementary and high schools shift to remote learning. The U.S. Department of Education adopted its own interpretation of how that money should be divvied up in a way that would significantly help private schools. Under the department’s rule, school districts have the option to send money to private schools based on their total student enrollment. Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have said that this runs contrary to the intent of the CARES Act, which said the money should be allocated based on the number of low-income students in each school. In July 2020, California joined Michigan, Maine, New Mexico, Wisconsin and Washington D.C. in a lawsuit. They argue that the department and its secretary Betsy Devos have overstepped their constitutional authority in ignoring the “plain language” of a bill passed by Congress and that the rule has neither a legal or a logical rationale.

nickname: Delayed debt relief for public service
proper_title: People of the State of California v. Betsy Devos
case_summary: In 2007, Congress passed the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, offering the following deal to indebted college graduates: get a job as a health care worker, a teacher or in some other designated public service while making regular payments on your loans for 10 years and the federal government will pay off the rest. But for years borrowers across the country have said that they’ve been denied relief through the program despite following the rules. Beginning in 2017, watchdogs within the federal government began sounding the alarm, accusing the Education Department, which administers the program, of routinely misleading applicants, mismanaging payments and ignoring complaints. In 2018, Congress passed what was supposed to be a quick fix, creating a new system that with a simplified application process: the Temporary Expanded Public Service Loan Forgiveness program. But according to California’s Attorney General, the Education Department is still effectively using the same application procedures and is denying 94% of all applicants. The state sued arguing that the department is unlawfully ignoring a clear mandate from Congress.

nickname: Pumping the brakes on the clean car rollback
proper_title: State of California v. Andrew Wheeler
case_summary: In 2010, the Obama administration came out with new fuel economy standards that require each auto manufacturer to increase the average gas mileage of its new cars by 5% each year. At the end of March 2020, the Trump administration announced that it would be loosening the required increase to 1.5% each year and easing up rules related to greenhouse gas emissions. California Attorney General Xavier Becerra threatened to sue at the time. Now he finally is, along with 23 other states and Washington DC. They argue that the new rules are contrary to federal environmental law and that they are based on sloppy analysis contrary to the regulations that governor how federal regulations must be introduced. While this case plays out, the state is also challenging the Trump administration’s argument that federal law override’s California’s stronger tailpipe emission standards (see: Saving the state's smog standards — Part 2).

nickname: Going easy on polluters during the pandemic
proper_title: State of New York v. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: On March 26, 2020, the Environmental Protection Agency’s chief compliance officer issued a memo to staff and regulated businesses announcing that for the duration of the pandemic the agency would be taking a softer approach to regulation and enforcement. If, for example, a business in unable to comply with routine environmental monitoring due to a lack of workers or laboratory capacity, “the EPA does not expect to seek penalties for violations,” the memo read. New York, California and seven other states sued arguing that the EPA doesn’t have the legal authority to ease up on regulations and that the new policy was introduced without following the federal law that governs how new regulations must be introduced.

nickname: Which Waters?, Round 3: A whole new rule
proper_title: State of California v. Andrew Wheeler
case_summary: In 2015, the Obama administration expanded the list of water ways protected by the federal Clean Water Act to include many wetlands and streams that pop up during rainstorms, to the chagrin of many farmers, oil producers, golf course owners and other pesticide and industrial chemical users across the country. In February 2018, the Environmental Protection Agency suspended the rule; New York, California and half a dozen other states plus Washington D.C. sued. Then in 2019, the Trump administration replaced the Obama-era rule entirely, reintroducing a standard from 1986. New York, California and a larger coalition of states and cities sued again. Now the Trump administration has introduced its own rule — narrower than both the Obama-era rule and the older standard. The same coalition of states is once again suing, arguing that the Trump administration did not provide sufficient justification for the new rule and that it misinterprets federal environmental law.

proper_title: State of California v. U.S. Department of Energy
case_summary: In February, the Trump administration's Department of Energy made it harder for its own agency bureaucrats to slap consumer appliances with tighter energy efficiency requirements. Under the new rule, the Department of Energy can only begin introducing a new efficiency standard if they meet a significantly higher energy savings standard. According to the department’s analysis, 40% of the efficiency standards introduced over the last three decades would not have passed muster under this new standard. California, along with 12 states, Washington DC and New York City, sued, arguing that there is no rationale basis for the higher standard.

proper_title: People of the State of California v. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration
case_summary: In January 2020, the Trump administration announced that California’s meal and rest break regulation do not apply to passenger-carrying commercial vehicles, such as tour bus companies, reasoning that they are overruled by less stringent federal laws and “would cause an unreasonable burden on interstate commerce.” California regulations entitle drivers to a 30-minute meal break every five hours. The state sued arguing that California state law is not in fact more stringent, that it enhances public safety and that it does not impose a burden on commerce.

proper_title: State of California v. Donald J. Trump
case_summary: In mid-February 2020, the Trump administration announced that it would redirecting $3.8 billion from the Defense Department to pay for the construction of the US-Mexico border wall. Much of the funding had been appropriated by Congress to purchase new equipment for the National Guard. California and 18 other states sued, arguing that the Constitution gives Congress, not the president, the sole right to appropriate federal funds. They also argue that the president's decision was made without following the proper administrative and environmental checks and procedures. If this all sounds familiar, it's because last year the Trump administration attempted the same fiscal switcheroo and California, along with 15 other states, sued. In June 2020, the Ninth District Court of Appeals ruled against the Trump administration.

proper_title: State of New York v. U.S. Department of Energy
case_summary: Maybe you remember the last time New York, California, and more than a dozen other states and cities sued the federal government over light bulbs. They’re doing it again, this time prompted by a December ruling from the Energy Department that it would not be imposing tighter energy efficiency standards on incandescent bulbs. The 14 states, along with Washington D.C. and New York City, sued, arguing that a law passed by Congress in 2007 requires the Department to set a certain efficiency standard requirement.

proper_title: State of New York v. Eugene Scalia
case_summary: Should McDonald’s be on the hook for labor violations carried out by its franchisees? What about a tech company that hires a janitorial subcontracting service that rips off its own workers? In 2016, the Obama administration introduced new standards making it harder for companies to wriggle out of “joint employment status,” putting them partially on the hook for violations against franchise workers, temp staffers and other contractors working in the company’s name. In January, the Trump administration introduced a rule rolling back those regulations making it easier for companies to shield themselves from joint employment liability. New York, California, 15 states and Washington D.C. sued, arguing that the new interpretation violations national labor law and that the Department of Labor failed to justify why the change was necessary.

nickname: Health risks to San Bernardino residents
proper_title: State of California v. Federal Aviation Administration
case_summary: The San Bernardino-Muscoy community has high asthma rates and the California Air Resources Board has deemed the area disproportionately burdened by pollution. In December, the Federal Aviation Administration approved an airport expansion project over a mile east of the San Bernardino-Muscoy community. California is suing the Federal Aviation Administration, the San Bernardino International Airport Authority, and Hillwood Enterprises, L.P. (the developer of the project). Attorney General Becerra says the agencies have ignored months of warnings of significant health risks that the project poses to area residents. California argues the Federal Aviation Administration failed to comply with the National Environmental Policy Act by approving the project.

proper_title: California Natural Resources Agency v. Wilbur Ross
case_summary: The Trump administration waded deeper into California’s water wars — a political conflict that, in one form or another, predates the state itself — by proposing to divert more water out of the Sacramento and San Joaquin River Delta to farmers in the Central Valley. California state agencies sued, arguing that the change would jeopardize fragile ecosystems and various fish species protected by the federal Endangered Species Act. They also argued that the federal government’s claim to the contrary and its break from a decade-long scientific assessment was made without justification and without giving the comment “a meaningful opportunity to comment.” Later that year, an industry group representing Pacific coast fisherman filed a very similar suit against the federal government. In May 2020, a judge sided with the state ordering federal regulators to put their new pumping regime on hold through the end of May, when the juvenile smelt are thought to be particularly vulnerable.

proper_title: State of California v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
case_summary: The Affordable Care Act (which you might know as “Obamacare”) allows people who don't get health insurance from their employer or the government to buy coverage on a statewide insurance marketplace, where lower-income buyers receive federal subsidies. Because Federal law bans taxpayer dollars from being used to cover abortions in most cases, since Obamacare was passed, insurance companies have been required to maintain separate financial accounts to cover those services. But in December 2019, the Trump administration added another restriction: insurance companies are now required to send customers separate invoices — one for coverage for abortion and one for everything else. In a statement, Health and Human Services Secretary Alex Azar said the new regulation “reflects President Trump’s strong commitment to preventing taxpayer funding of abortion coverage.” California, where health insurers are required to cover abortion, sued, along with five states and Washington D.C. They argue that the new rule is a “an irrational and onerous regulatory scheme that singles out and limits access to a critical women’s healthcare procedure,” that it violates each state’s right to set its own health care policy and that it was written and enacted in a way that violates the federal law that governs how new regulations must be introduced.

proper_title: State of Washington v. United States Department of State
case_summary: On March 26, 2020, the Environmental Protection Agency’s chief compliance officer issued a memo to staff and regulated businesses announcing that for the duration of the pandemic the agency would be taking a softer approach to regulation and enforcement. If, for example, a business in unable to comply with routine environmental monitoring due to a lack of workers or laboratory capacity, “the EPA does not expect to seek penalties for violations,” the memo read. New York, California and seven other states sued arguing that the EPA doesn’t have the legal authority to ease up on regulations and that the new policy was introduced without following the federal law that govern how new regulations must be introduced.

proper_title: State of California v. Joe Stout
case_summary: Since the George W. Bush administration, federal land managers and environmental activists have been duking it out in court over whether public land in Central California should be opened up to oil and gas drillers. In December 2019, the Trump administration’s Bureau of Land Management weighed in, issuing a new management plan for a swath of California spanning Fresno, Kern, Kings, Madera, San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara, Tulare and Ventura counties. Like the plans issued under the Bush and Obama administrations, the Trump plan would allow for oil and gas exploration. The state sued, arguing that the administration did not consider the full scope of possible environmental impacts, plan for those impacts, consider reasonable alternatives, allow for enough public comment or take California state law into account.

proper_title: District of Columbia v. United States Department of Agriculture
case_summary: Federal law requires all able-bodied adults who are under 50 and have no dependent children to work at least 20 hours per week or be enrolled in vocational training before to receive food stamps consistently. Otherwise, they can only get three months of food stamps every three years. But for at least a decade, most social service agencies in California have received permission from the federal government to waive that requirement. In December 2019, the Trump administration's Department of Agriculture announced that it would be tightening up the work requirement. The California Department of Justice estimates that 55,000 of the state's residents could lose access to food stamps within the first year. Joining 13 other states, Washington DC and New York City, California sued. The states argue that the new regulation, set to go into effect April 2020, violates existing federal law and the original intent of Congress and that the Trump administration failed to offer a reasonable justification for the change in policy.

nickname: Which Waters?, Round 2: What's old is new again
proper_title: State of New York v. Andrew Wheeler
case_summary: In 2015, the Obama administration expanded the list of water ways protected by the federal Clean Water Act. In February 2018, the Environmental Protection Agency suspended the rule; New York, California and half a dozen other states plus Washington D.C. sued. Now the Trump administration has officially replaced that water way rule entirely, reintroducing the old standard. New York, California and a larger coalition of states and cities are suing again. They argue that the Trump administration did not provide sufficient justification for the new rule, that it failed to give the public enough time to weigh in and that the new regulations (that is, the old regulations) don’t comply with a series of recent Supreme Court decisions.

nickname: Saving the state's smog standards — Part 2
proper_title: State of California v. Andrew Wheeler
case_summary: Stop us if you've heard this one before. Remember when California and a coalition of states and cities sued the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration in September of 2019 for ruling that the state's stricter auto emissions rules were preempted by federal law? (If not, see "Saving the state's smog standards — Part 1"). California, along with the same coalition, sued again — this time targeting the Environmental Protection Agency for its decision to revoke parts of the waiver that allow California to restrict greenhouse gases in tailpipe pollution and require that automakers sell clean cars in the state.

proper_title: State of New York v. U.S. Department of Energy
case_summary: California, along with New York and 13 other states, are suing the federal government over light bulbs. In the final days of the Obama administration, the Department of Energy slapped heightened energy efficiency guidelines on certain lamp manufacturers, effectively phasing out energy-intensive incandescent lightbulbs. The Trump administration reversed the rule in September of this year, citing higher costs for both consumers and producers. The states argue that the new rule violates federal energy law as well as the rules that govern how new regulations are supposed to be enacted.

proper_title: State of California v. David Bernhardt
case_summary: California has over 300 species considered endangered or threatened, including the California condor and the grizzly bear. In August of 2019, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service finalized rules changing how the federal Endangered Species Act is enforced — rolling back protections given to threatened species, and for the first time allowing government officials to consider the economic impact of protecting a new species. In its suit, California, along with 18 other states and the city of New York, contend the new rules are unlawful under the National Environmental Policy Act and undermine the purpose of the Endangered Species Act.

nickname: Saving the state's smog standards — Part 1
proper_title: State of California v. Elaine Chao
case_summary: In 2012, California adopted its Advanced Clean Cars Program to reduce smog and greenhouse gas polution, and boost electric vehicle sales in the state. The state has maintained tighter anti-smog standards for half a century thanks to a series of special waivers from Washington. In September, President Trump announced (on Twitter, naturally) that his Department of Transportation had concluded that federal law superceded the state's stricted standards. California and 22 other states, along with Washington D.C., Los Angeles and New York City, sued. They argue that the administration exceeded its authority, that the decision was made without sufficient explanation or justification and that it violates federal environmental law. In February 2020, a federal judge put the case on hold while a related challenged filed by the Union of Concerned Scientists plays out in court.

nickname: Best Interest rule not the best?
proper_title: State of New York v. United States Securities and Exchange Commission
case_summary: In June of 2019, the Securities and Exchange Commission, the federal agency that regulates capital markets, introduced a new rule requiring stock brokers to act in the "best interest" of their clients when recommending a particular investment (rather than be motivated by, say, the size of a commission on a sale). But the Trump administration's new rule stops short of an earlier regulation introduced by the Obama administration known as the "fiduciary rule." California, seven states and Washington D.C. sued, arguing that the new, weaker regulation violates the Dodd-Frank Act, a package of financial regulationspassed in the aftermath of the financial crisis which requires that brokers and investment advisors be subject to the same conflict of interest rules.

nickname: Fighting for Flores and against detaining children
proper_title: State of California v. Kevin K. McAleenan
case_summary: In the late summer of 2019, the Trump administration announced a new policy that would allow undocumented children to be detained for as long as it takes to adjudicate their immigration claim unless a parent or legal guardian is available to care for them. The new policy is at odds with Flores Settlement, a legal agreement struck in 1997 between the federal government and the American Civil Liberties Union, which put a 20-day cap on how long immigration authorities can detain undocumented children before being released to a guardian or adult relative. Along with 19 states and the District of Columbia, California sued. In a 126-page complaint, the states argue that the new rule is neither well-reasoned nor logically justified and therefore represents an abuse of federal regulatory discretion, that it constitutes a "usurpation of traditional state authority" over childcare and welfare and that the policy of long-term detention violates the due process rights of undocumented immigrants.

proper_title: State of New York v. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: The “Clean Power Plan,” one of the signature environmental policies of the Obama administration, set greenhouse gas reduction targets for electricity generators in each state with the ultimate goal of cutting national power plant emissions by 32% by 2030. In July of 2019, the Trump administration formally scrapped the Clean Power Plan and replaced it with a plan of its own: the “Affordable Clean Energy rule.” Under the new plan, emissions would fall by roughly 1%, a reduction that would come mostly from production efficiency gains. Under the Obama plan, states were encouraged to adopt carbon pricing, reduce the use of high-carbon fuel sources like coal and capture emissions. Alongside 21 states and seven cities, California is suing, arguing that the new rule violate the federal Clean Air Act which the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 2006 requires the Environmental Protection Action to regulate climate-warming gasses.

proper_title: State of New York v. Andrew Wheeler
case_summary: In July 2019, the Environmental Protection Agency gave farmers the final go-ahead to spray their crops with chlorpyrifos (klor-PEER-i-foss), an insecticide that has been linked to neurological delays in children and has been banned from home use. California and five other states sued, arguing that the EPA did not make a compelling case that the insecticide is safe and that the agency’s own scientists have been unable to determine a safe level of exposure. This is part of a decade-long debate. Environmental activists have been fighting in the courts since 2007 hoping to force federal regulators to ban chlorpyrifos. Though the Obama Administration finally agreed in 2015, the Trump administration reversed that decision two months after the president took office. California and the five other states objected and, after months of delay, the Trump administration finally announced that they would be ignoring that objection. Hence the lawsuit.

proper_title: State of New York v. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
case_summary: Federal environmental regulators require car manufacturers to meet average fuel-economy standards, meaning that each company's fleet has to exceed certain average miles-per-gallon. In 2016, the Obama administration passed a new rule arguing that the penalties automakers are forced to pay if they fall below those standards should have been inching up with inflation since the 1990's. To catch up, regulators hiked the per-car cost from $5.50 for every tenth of a mile-per-gallon that the fleet falls below the federal standard to $14. In July, 2019, the Trump administration attempted to roll back that inflation adjustment, resetting the penalty to $5.50. New York, California and 11 other states sued, arguing a 2015 federal law requires fuel economy penalties to be subject to inflation-adjustments. This follows a 2017 legal battle in which the Trump administration attempted to delay implementation of the Obama-era rule, but lost in court.

proper_title: State of California v. U.S. Department of Transportation
case_summary: In his state of the state speech, Gov. Gavin Newsom “leveled” with Californians, announcing that “there simply isn’t a path” to complete the state-spanning high-speed rail project anytime soon and that his administration would instead focus on connecting Merced and Bakersfield. Noting that the federal government had kicked some $3.5 billion into the project, President Trump responded on Twitter: “We want that money back now.” In mid-May of 2019, the U.S. Federal Railroad Administration made good on that threat—at least in part—by announcing that it would be clawing back a $929 million construction grant. The administration argued that the project was hopelessly behind schedule and that the governor had unilaterally changed its scope. A week later, the governor, through the state’s attorney general, sued, arguing that the federal government did not give the state enough time to resolve any disagreements, a violation of federal procedural rules.

proper_title: States of New York v. United States Department of Agriculture
case_summary: In 2018, the Trump administration’s Department of Agriculture weakened a set of national nutritional standards requiring public schools to cut the use of sodium and increase the use of whole-grains in the breakfasts and lunches they serves to students. Six states and Washington D.C. sued, arguing that the new rule violates federal law requiring school meal requirements to be made “on the basis of tested nutritional research.” They also argued that the rule was introduced without giving the states the opportunity to weigh in.

nickname: Methane Waste Flare Up, Third Time's a Charm
proper_title: State of California v. Ryan Zinke
case_summary: Last July, New Mexico and California teamed up to sue the Trump administration for slow-walking an Obama-era regulation designed to limit methane emissions from oil and gas drilling operations on public land. A judge agreed with the states. Then in December, the administration announced plans to suspend certain provisions of the rule. The duo of western states sued and won again. Finally, last month, the Environmental Protection Agency announced that it would ditching the "Waste Prevention Rule" entirely. So for the third time, the two states are back in court again, arguing that the federal government failed to provide a reasonable justification and is in violation of federal environmental regulations.

proper_title: State of New York v. U.S. Department of the Interior
case_summary: For decades, the federal government has used the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, a century-old international agreement, to criminally prosecute utilities, oil companies and other big industries for engaging in business activities that kill or maim certain migratory birds, including bald eagles. Last December, the Trump administration revised its interpretation of the treaty, arguing that companies should be let off the hook as long as they don’t intentionally set out to harm birds. Eight states, including California, say that this violates both the letter and the spirit of the treaty and are now suing. This lawsuit follows a similar case brought by conservation groups, including the National Audubon Society.

proper_title: People of the State of California v. International Boundary and Water Commission
case_summary: In September of 2019, the State of California sued the United States office of the International Boundary and Water Commission, a joint U.S.-Mexico agency tasked with regulating wastewater that flows across the border. The State's Attorney General filed the suit on behalf of the San Diego regional Water Board, arguing that the Commission has allowed millions of gallons of sewage and pesticide-laced water to flow into the United States, violating the Clean Water Act.

proper_title: State of Washington v. United States Department of State
case_summary: Defense Distributed is a Texas-based non-profit that specializes in the design and development of digital firearm blueprints that can be used to produce untraceable guns with a 3D printer. In 2015, the U.S. State Department blocked the firm from publishing its DIY gun designs online, but in July the federal government settled the legal dispute, allowing the company to publish of its open-source, printable gun codes. The State of Washington, along with seven other states, sued, arguing that the release of the codes violate their rights to regulate firearms within their own borders. A federal judge placed a temporary restraining order on the codes five days after their publication, which—after a motion for a preliminary injuction filed August 10—will continue until August 28. California now joins the lawsuit.

proper_title: State of New York v. E. Scott Pruitt
case_summary: Hydrofluorocarbons are chemical refrigerants that, ironically, also happen to be powerful contributors to global warming. Last year, a court overturned an Obama-era regulation that banned the production and use of all HFCs, but left open the possibility that federal regulators could restrict any new uses of the chemical class. Instead, the Environmental Protection Agency announced that it be dropping the restriction entirely. Eleven states plus Washington D.C. sued, arguing that the agency did not provide an adequate justification for this decision.

proper_title: State of Washington v. The United States of America
case_summary: Last April, the U.S. Justice Department announced that it would be prosecuting anyone who crosses the border illegally, including those who come with children. Because the government cannot legally keep children in restrictive immigration detention facilities for extended periods of time, the Trump administration enforced this “zero tolerance” policy by separating children from their parents or guardians. After a massive public outcry, President Trump signed an executive order asking the courts to allow the administration to detain families together. Washington State and sixteen other states sued, arguing that the separation policy violates the due process rights of parents and children. They also argue that President Trump’s order does not help reunite the families that have already been separated and, because the order requires court approval to be enforced, “fails to provide any actual relief.”

proper_title: State of California v. United States Environmental Protection Agency and E. Scott Pruitt
case_summary: Under the Obama administration, the Environmental Protection Agency established a single emissions standard for all U.S. cars. The rule required a 45.4 miles per gallon average by 2022 and more than 50 miles per gallon by 2025. But this April, the E.P.A. led by administrator Scott Pruitt announced that it would be rolling the standards back. California, and 16 other states, plus the District of Columbia, sued, arguing that the decision lacked a rational basis and that it violated the Clean Air Act.

proper_title: State of California v. United States Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: Since 1995 the Environmental Protection Agency has followed the “once in, always in” rule in regulating hazardous air pollution. Once a power plant or refinery is classified as a “major source” of dangerous pollution, it is saddled with strict environmental standards—and those standards are never lifted. In January of 2018, the EPA announced that it would be rescinding the rule. California sued, arguing that this contradicts the intent of the Clean Air Act.

proper_title: State of New York v. E. Scott Pruitt
case_summary: In March of 2017, the EPA announced that it would be reversing an Obama-era environmental policy and no longer asking the oil and gas industry to collect methane emission data. Fourteen states has now sued the agency, arguing the Clean Air Act requires federal regulators to set informed methane emission guidelines for existing oil and gas industry.

proper_title: State of California v. U.S. Department of Justice and Office of Justice Programs
case_summary: After the Trump administration decided to cut off designated "sanctuary" jurisdictions from some federal law enforcement grants, California filed a Freedom of Information Act request to learn more about the decision. The Trump administration ignored the request and so California responded with a lawsuit.

proper_title: State of New York v. E. Scott Pruitt
case_summary: In 2015, the Obama administration expanded the number of water ways protected by federal environmental regulation. President Trump ordered his Environmental Protection Agency to review the law, which they did and then suspended. California, and a few other states, responded with a lawsuit.

proper_title: State of California v. Joseph Balash
case_summary: Late last year, the Trump administration repealed a 2015 Obama rule that put tighter restrictions on oil and gas drillers operating on Native American land. Attorney General Becerra argued that the federal regulators hadn't provided a good enough legal justification for the repeal and sued.

proper_title: State of New York v. Federal Communications Commission
case_summary: Last December, the Federal Communications Commission repealed an Obama-era "net neutrality" rule, which prevented internet service providers from selectively blocking or slowing down access to some websites over others. Twenty two states, including California, sued, arguing that the rule change was an overreach of the commission's power.

proper_title: People of California v. U.S. Department of Education
case_summary: Though a court found that thousands of former students at the for-profit Corinthian Colleges were entitled to debt relief, the federal Department of Education has yet to process their claims. Attorney General Becerra filed a lawsuit on behalf 38,000 Californians.

proper_title: Stockman v. Trump
case_summary: After President Trump announced a new ban on transgender servicemembers in the military, seven men and women sued the administration along with a group of LGBTQ rights organizations. The State of California has since joined the suit.

proper_title: Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security
case_summary: Massachusetts, California, and eight other states requested information from the Department on Homeland Security to find out what exactly immigration enforcement officials are up to within their various jurisdictions. When the administration ignored the request, the states sued.

proper_title: State of Maryland v. U.S. Department of Education
case_summary: Seventeen states sued the Department of Education for delaying the enactment of an Obama-era regulation requiring colleges to meet “accountability standards” based on student debt load, graduation rates, and post-graduate employment.

proper_title: State of California v. Donald J. Trump
case_summary: The Affordable Care Act mandates that insurance companies offer low out-of-pocket cost plans to certain low earners. Since the law was enacted, the federal government has compensated insurance companies for this additional cost. When President Trump announced that his administration would no longer be making those payments, California and 17 other states plus Washington, D.C., sued. The following year, the Trump administration announced that it would allow insurance companies to hike insurance premiums on those plans, effectively forcing the federal government to pick up the extra cost through premium subsidies. California asked the courts to put the suit on hold…for now.

proper_title: State of California v. Hargan
case_summary: After the Trump administration made it easier for employers to deny their employees insurance coverage for contraception, California sued, alleging that it discriminated against women and violated the first amendment’s separation of church and state. The final rules are set to go into effect in early January. Since the initial filing, a dozen states have joined the lawsuit.

nickname: Conflict of Interest at the EPA
proper_title: State of California v. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: Before he was the head of the Environmental Protection Agency, Scott Pruitt was the Attorney General of Oklahoma, where he sued the EPA 14 times. Once in D.C., did Pruit help draft rules related to the very suits he once filed? California Attorney General Becerra wanted to know, and when the EPA failed to produce the requested documents, he sued. When Pruit resigned in July of 2018, the EPA settled without admitting guilt (though they did pay California's legal bills).

proper_title: Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Education
case_summary: Nineteen states sued the Department of Education for refusing to enact a rule from 2016 intended to make it easier for students to have their loans forgiven if they attend colleges that engage in fraud. The states argued that the Department did not provide a legal or rational justification for its decision and failed to solicit public comment.

proper_title: State of California v. U.S. Bureau of Land Management
case_summary: Last November the Obama administration came up with a rule designed to limit methane emissions from oil and gas drilling operations on public land. The Trump administration didn’t implement the rule, so California and New Mexico sued, arguing that the feds were violating legal rulemaking processes. A judge sided with the states.

proper_title: State of California v. Zinke
case_summary: California, along with three other states, sued the federal government after Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke repealed an Obama-era moratorium on leasing federal land for coal mining. The case has since been merged with another legal challenge brought by the environmental group, Citizens for Clean Energy. After a court ruled that the Trump administration could not lift the lease ban without conducting a full environmental review, the Department of Interior issued its analysis. The four states were not impressed and updated their lawsuit, arguing that the environmental impact statement failed to consider many likely environmental impacts.

proper_title: State of Washington v. Trump
case_summary: After the courts swatted down President Trump’s first travel ban, the White House issued a second, slightly less restrictive version hoping that it would pass legal muster. No such luck. In fact, there were so many separate challenges to the new ban that this case, filed by Washington’s Attorney General Bob Ferguson and five other states including California, didn’t even get its day in court. Once judges in Maryland and Hawaii put separate freezes on the new policy, this complaint was put on hold indefinitely.

proper_title: State of California v. Andrew R. Wheeler
case_summary: In March of 2019, the federal Environmental Protection Agency determined that the Redwood City Salt Ponds, owned by the Agribusiness Giant Cargill, are not regulated under the national Clean Water Act. The decision would make it much easier to dredge, fill and develop the 1,365 acre site just south of San Francisco. California is now suing, arguing that federal environmental regulators exceeded their authority, misinterpreted the Clean Water Act and did not offer sufficient evidence to justify the decision. The court ruled against the Trump Administration and found that the EPA ignored its own regulations.

nickname: No green cards for welfare users
proper_title: State of California v. Department of Homeland Security
case_summary: In August of 2019, the Trump administration announced new rules that would make it harder for immigrants to get green cards if they use — or are deemed likely to use — social safety net programs like food stamps and Medicaid. This modifies an existing rule which has typically been applied to immigrants who are believed to become fully financially dependent on the state, rather than those who temporarily make use of specific social services. California, along with three states and Washington D.C., filed a lawsuit arguing that the new standard disproportionately targets immigrants from low-income, mainly non-white majority countries, a violation of their equal protection rights. Attorneys General from the plaintiffs also argue that the rule violates both immigration law and the rules that govern how new regulations must be introduced. In late January 2020, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Trump administration would be allowed to impliment its new policy while the legal challenge works its way through the courts.

proper_title: State of California v. United States Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: Federal law requires manufacturers and importers to report their use of asbestos, a carcinogen, to the Environmental Protection Agency. In January of 2019, California and 14 other states, asked the agency to eliminate what the states’ attorneys general said are loopholes in those federal reporting requirements that exempt asbestos processors and importers of raw asbestos. The EPA rejected the petition saying that they are able to gather the necessary information in other ways. Now the states are taking the agency to court.

proper_title: State of California v. Alex M. Azar
case_summary: In early May of 2019, the Trump administration issued a new rule expanding the ability of medical providers that receive federal medical funding to refuse to provide certain health care services by claiming a religious or moral objection. The rule has been protested by abortion and LGBTQ rights groups. The State Attorney General’s office sued a few weeks later arguing that, among other things, the rule violates the first amendment’s restriction on laws “respecting an establishment of religion” and that the federal government’s threat to withhold medical funds from the state if it does not comply is a breach of executive authority. A district court judge sided with the state in November of 2019.

proper_title: State of California v. Alex M. Azar
case_summary: In early May of 2019, the Trump administration introduced a new rule prohibiting states from using Medicaid payments to pay unions (in the form of, say, union dues) who represent groups of medical providers. There are half a million unionized homecare workers in California who are paid by Medi-Cal, the state’s Medicaid program. California sued along with four other states that have similar programs. In their lawsuit, the states accused the Department of Health and Human Services of trying to “reinterpret the Medicaid Act in service of anti-union objectives.”

proper_title: State of California v. Donald Trump
case_summary: In mid-February 2019, President Trump signed a Declaration of National Emergency ordering that nearly $7 billion designated for military construction and drug enforcement operations be used instead for the construction of additional border fencing. A few days later—on President’s Day—California sued the administration along with 15 other states. The suit argued that the president doesn’t have the constitutional authority to shift around money appropriated by Congress and, anyhow, that there is no real emergency on the southern border, making the emergency declaration invalid. To back up that second point, the suit includes a statement the president made when announcing the declaration: “I could do the wall over a longer period of time. I didn’t need to do this. But I’d rather do it much faster.” On June 26, 2020, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals agreed. In his opinion, the circuit court's chief justice wrote that "there was no unanticipated crisis at the border" and that "(n)othing prevented Congress from funding solutions to this problem through the ordinary appropriations process — Congress simply chose not to fund this particular solution."

proper_title: State of California v. Jefferson B. Sessions
case_summary: For the second year in a row, the Trump's Justice Department has decided to withhold certain grant money from designed “sanctuary” jurisdictions unless and until they agree to allow their law enforcement officers to cooperate with federal immigration agents. A district judge ruled against the administration, and on July 13, 2020, the Ninth District Court of Appeals agreed. The panel of judges ruled that the Trump administration had abused its authority in withholding the funds and that the "sanctuary" policies of the California cities involved did not violate federal law. Last year, California sued over similar restrictions and won.

proper_title: State of New York v. U.S. Department of Labor
case_summary: In October 2017, after Congressional Republicans failed in their attempt to repeal the Affordable Care Act, President Trump issued an executive order that eased rules put into place by that act. In January, the Department of Labor adopted a policy that allows employers to join together to form Association Health Plans, which operate outside of the ACA insurance market—and without the consumer protections of the ACA. Becerra and the 12 states he joined in this suit say that this change represents another step in the administration’s plan to neuter the Obama healthcare act and puts consumers at risk by driving up the price of coverage. A lower court judge agreed with the states and ordered the Department of Labor to try again.

proper_title: State of California v. United States Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: In July 2018, the Environmental Protection Agency announced that it would suspend an Obama-era rule that set strict limits on the number of remanufactured heavy-duty "glider trucks" that could be sold each year. Glider trucks have a used engine in a new frame and emit up to 450 times more diesel particulate matter and up to 40 times more smog-forming nitrogen oxides than new trucks. Californial leads a coalition of 16 states suing the administration to restore the rule, citing the adverse impact of these pollutants on health and the environment.

proper_title: State of California v. United States Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: In October 2016, the Obama administration introduced new rules aimed at controlling greenhouse gas emissions from municipal landfills. California, and seven other states, are sued the Environmental Protection Agency, arguing that under the leadership of President Trump, the agency has not only ignored the rules, but "worked to undermine them." The court agreed.

proper_title: States of New York, California, and Maryland v. E. Scott Pruitt
case_summary: In 2015, President Obama's Environmental Protection Agency strengthened a rule that requires agricultural companies to train their workers on how to minimize their exposure to pesticides. The Trump administration suspended that beefed up training requirement last December. Three states have sued, arguing that the federal government offered no legal justification for its decision. A month later the EPA released new standards and the states ended their legal challenge.

proper_title: State of California v. Wilbur L. Ross
case_summary: Every ten years, the federal government conducts a census to better understand the population and decide how to divvy up Congressional representation and federal funding. In March, the Department of Commerce announced that they would be re-introducing a question about citizenship on the 2020 census—a practice abandoned in 1950—arguing that it will allow for better enforcement of the Voting Rights Act. California sued, arguing that the new question would discourage undocumented immigrants from participating and that the U.S. Constitution demands an accurate population count, regardless of citizenship. A lower court ruled for California and the federal government has appealed.

proper_title: State of California v. United States Bureau of Land Management and Katharine S. MacGregor
case_summary: After losing a case to California and New Mexico over its failure to implement an Obama-era environmental rule on methane emissions, the BLM suspended a part of the new rule. California and New Mexico sued again. A court agreed to put the change on hold.

proper_title: State of California v. Scott Pruitt
case_summary: In 2015, the Obama administration announced new rules requires federal environmental regulators to identify areas of the country with polluted air. Despite an earlier court ruling, the EPA decided not to. California, plus 13 states and Washington D.C., sued and won. In March of 2018, the EPA agreed to write new rules.

proper_title: State of California v. U.S. Department of the Interior
case_summary: California and New Mexico sued the Trump administration for repealing a new method of calculating how much money energy companies must pay to state governments when they drill or mine on public land. The states argue that the Trump administration “failed to supply a reasoned basis” when it decided to overturn the rule.

proper_title: People of the State of California v. U.S. Department of Transportation
case_summary: California and seven other states sued the administration for dragging its feet in implementing a new set of rules that would require transportation officials to track greenhouse gas emissions along national highways and set environmental sustainability performance goals. The Federal Highway Administration decided to enact the rule, but has since proposed repealing it.

proper_title: State of California v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security
case_summary: California filed a lawsuit with three other states after President Trump announced that he would be ending the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, which allowed those who entered the United States illegally as minors to remain on a temporary basis. This case was consolidated with a number of other similar challenges, including one brought by the regents of the University of California. On June 17, 2020 the U.S. Supreme Court sided against the Trump administration, arguing that it did not offer a sufficiently detailed justification for its decision to end the program.

proper_title: State of New York v. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
case_summary: Five states sued the Trump administration’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration for failing to enact a congressionally mandated rule that would have increased the penalty charged to car manufacturers for violating average-gas-mileage standards. A court agreed and mandated that the rule go into effect.

proper_title: State of California v. Sessions
case_summary: California sued Trump's Justice Department after the administration announced plans to cut off designed “sanctuary” jurisdictions from certain federal funding programs unless they cooperate with federal immigration agents. After a district court ruled in late November, 2018, that the funding cuts were unconstitutional, California asked that the same ruling be applied to yet another law enforcement grant that the Trump administration had pulled from the state.

proper_title: State of New York v. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
case_summary: One August 1, 15 states sued the Environmental Protection Agency for postponing a regulation designed to combat smog. On August 2, EPA chief Scott Pruitt reversed course.

nickname: Freezers and Coolers and Boilers (Oh My)
proper_title: State of California v. Perry
case_summary: The Obama administration directed the Department of Energy to come up with new energy efficiency requirements for freezers, air conditioners, and other appliances. The Trump administration never got around to finalizing those rules, so California and ten other states sued.

proper_title: People of the State of California v. U.S. Department of the Interior
case_summary: Last year the Obama administration rolled out a new method for calculating how much money energy companies owe state governments for the right to drill or mine on public land. The Trump administration delayed implementation of the rule, so California and New Mexico sued. A district judge sided with the states—just in time for the Trump administration to repeal it outright.

proper_title: State of New York v. Perry
case_summary: In the final days of the Obama administration, the Department of Energy rolled out a series of new energy efficiency requirements for ceiling fans. The new rules were supposed to go into effect in March, but the Trump administration delayed. Then they delayed again. After 10 state attorneys general sued, the Department of Energy relented and OKed the standards.
